newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RUGBY UNION-AUSTRALIA PAYS HIGH PRICE OF PROFESSIONALISM.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-AUSTRALIA PAYS HIGH PRICE OF PROFESSIONALISM.

text.p: Former Wallaby captain Phil Kearns was still smiling last year even though he missed the entire season because of a serious ankle injury.

Under a lucrative three-year contract, the burly front rower was guaranteed full pay regardless of his fitness or form. Not even being dropped by Australia, or New South Wales, could affect his reported A$300,000 ($228,000) annual salary.

The pay guarantee, which covered the 26-man Wallaby squad of the day, has proved a significant financial burden for the Australian Rugby Union (ARU) since the game turned professional in 1995, but attempts to overhaul the contract system are now floundering amid opposition from the players.
Rather than focus on the test against France in Sydney on June 21, Australian rugby is preparing for a showdown in the courts.

The first of the original Wallaby contracts expire at the end of 1997 and, while the ARU are determined to claw back some of the concessions they made, the players are equally determined to protect hard-won gains.

At the heart of the dispute is the players' insistence the ARU granted them a legally-binding veto over the distribution of television broadcast rights money between Australia's three states -- Queensland, New South Wales and ACT.
The ruling body disagreed and when the players' financial direction was ignored by the ARU, they began legal action against their employers in a case that has yet to go to court.
Kearns believes his colleagues will fight hard to retain what they believe are their legal rights -- and the bargaining power they bring with them.
"I don't think the players will back down and nor should they back down," he said.

As captain, Kearns ruffled the establishment by supporting a failed bid by the rebel World Rugby Corporation organisation to take control of the sport in 1995 by signing Australian, New Zealand and South African internationals. It was also a time when rich rugby league clubs were looking to poach leading players.
Threatened on two fronts, the ARU acted quickly to secure the sport's prize asset, the players. Without them, the officials argued, their future was bleak.

The union had already joined forces with their counterparts in New Zealand and South Africa. The three nations sold the broadcast rights for 10 years of all tests between the countries and the provincial Super 12 competition for US$550 million to media tycoon Rupert Murdoch.

To secure the players, the ARU promised to spend 95 percent of their television revenue on players' wages. In addition, two players, one with voting rights, joined the ARU board. These were decisions the ARU would quickly regret.
"I think it took the ARU about one month to realise just how much power they had given away to secure the players," said Players' Association president and former test flanker Tony Dempsey.
"We knew we had strength and we knew we had to take advantage of that position as quickly as possible. The ARU was vulnerable at the time," Kearns recalled.
According to Matt Carroll, general manager, rugby, at the ARU, there was little time for reflection in such pressing circumstances. Delay, he said, could have been fatal.
"Of course, decisions were rushed. But at least we kept control of our sport," Carroll said.
"It was crisis management in 1995. There was a rush to get signatures. There was no doubt that the day for re-negotiating with the players would come. No agreement is written in stone."
A collective bargaining deal would involve a switch to a mix of signing-on fees and bonuses for tests appearances and the disappearance of fixed payments like the ones an idle Kearns enjoyed in 1996.
In return, the players would secure minimum salary for Super 12 players and enhanced employment rights among other benefits.
But the sticking point remains the players' disputed right of veto.
"We will fight to retain that say. It is very important to maintain an area that players are properly represented or we will be walked over," Dempsey said.
